# RFC-0005: Coordinate interpretation and point references

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `crs`, `architecture`, `io-format`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0005:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0005c-overview"></a>

Two questions turn out to be the same question: *what does this coordinate mean*, and *which point is
this*. Both are answered relative to a particular source at a particular version, both are meaningless
if that source is silently replaced, and both produce failures that are invisible on inspection — a
vertical datum error shifts every canopy height by a smooth plausible constant, and a stale point
reference names a different point while resolving perfectly.

**Scope** — how a coordinate reference system is carried and compared; where transformation capability
comes from; what may be transformed and what may not; vertical datum handling; what a committed result
guarantees when transformation implementations differ; what a point reference is and where it may be
used; and how a source is bound to the version a reference was taken against.

**Out of scope** — which projections or grid files are supported, and the transformation implementations
themselves. Identity across *different* sources: a point in one flight is never the same point as one in
another. Joins to tabular data, which key on attributes rather than point references.

The design goal for both halves is deliberately narrow. Region edits ([RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 2) were shaped
precisely to avoid needing point identity, so identity is off the common path and need not be a
format-level guarantee. And coordinate transformation is a capability a library crate may not link
([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host)), so interpretation belongs to the host while library crates carry and compare.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0005:C-CRS] Coordinate reference systems as opaque metadata (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-crs"></a>

A library crate carries a coordinate reference system without understanding it. Interpreting one requires a
transformation database that a library crate may not open ([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 1), so interpretation is the
host's job and libraries are limited to carrying and comparing.

1. A source and every pipeline stage MUST carry the coordinate reference system of the coordinates it
   produces.
   - Where the data has a vertical reference, that MUST be carried too, distinguishably from the horizontal
     system.
2. A library crate MUST treat a coordinate reference system as opaque.
   - It MAY compare two for identity.
   - It MUST NOT otherwise parse, interpret, or infer from them.
3. Absence of a declared coordinate reference system MUST be represented distinctly from a declared one, and
   MUST NOT be defaulted to any particular system.

#### Rationale

(2) keeps interpretation where the authority is. Deciding whether two systems are *equivalent* — as opposed
to identical — requires the transformation database, so a library crate attempting it would either be wrong
or would need the filesystem access [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 1 forbids. Identity comparison is enough for the
library's actual need, which is detecting mismatch and refusing to proceed.

(3) exists because the convenient default is the dangerous one. LAS files frequently carry no usable
coordinate reference system, and assuming one — the project's, the last file's, a plausible local grid —
produces data that is confidently mislocated rather than obviously unusable. An absent system must propagate
as absent so that any operation requiring one fails rather than guessing.

### [RFC-0005:C-TRANSFORM] Transformation is host-supplied and applies to queries (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-transform"></a>

Reprojecting a point cloud is close to the worst available operation on one: per-point trigonometry over
billions of points, changing no information, and destroying the scaled-integer representation that makes
exact accumulation possible. The alternative is to transform what is small — bounds and outputs — and leave
the points alone.

1. A library crate MUST obtain coordinate transformation from a capability supplied by its caller, and MUST
   NOT link or invoke a transformation library directly.
2. Stored point coordinates MUST NOT be transformed as a side effect of querying, rendering, or displaying.
   - A query expressed in one system MUST instead be satisfied by transforming the query region into the
     source's system.
3. Transformation of point coordinates MUST occur only through an explicit operator.
   - Such an operator MUST declare zero halo width and a single pass ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1).
   - Conversion between vertical references is such a transformation and is subject to this item.
4. An operation combining sources whose coordinate reference systems are not identical MUST either include
   an explicit transformation operator or fail.
   - Where it fails, the failure MUST name the mismatch.
   - It MUST NOT transform implicitly to make the operation succeed.

#### Rationale

(2) is the substantive requirement. Transforming a viewport's bounds costs a handful of operations;
transforming the points it contains costs billions. Beyond cost, LAS and COPC store coordinates as scaled
integers, so reprojection requires requantisation — which is lossy and forfeits the bit-identity
[RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 2 requires, by moving aggregates from exact integer arithmetic onto floating point
where reduction order starts to matter. Keeping points in their native system also means references into
them stay valid, which is what C-IDENTITY relies on and the reason reprojection cannot orphan an edit.

(3) needs no new machinery: an explicit reprojection is position-independent, so declaring zero halo and one
pass makes it exact under extent restriction by [RFC-0003:C-RESOLUTION](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-resolution) 2. Applying a geoid model has the
same shape — a bounded grid summary broadcast over batches — which is why vertical conversion is folded in
here rather than specified separately.

(4) refuses the implicit conversion because the implicit conversion is how mismatches stop being visible. A
tool that quietly reprojects to make an operation succeed has removed the user's only signal that two
datasets were not comparable.

### [RFC-0005:C-VERTICAL] Vertical datums (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-vertical"></a>

This clause exists because of one specific wrong number. Ellipsoidal height and orthometric height differ by
tens of metres, varying geographically, so a vertical datum error shifts every height by a smooth plausible
offset — no artefact, no error, and a timber inventory that is uniformly wrong.

1. An operation whose result depends on height relative to a surface — height above ground, canopy metrics,
   terrain models, volume — MUST fail unless every input's vertical reference is established and identical.
   - Inputs whose vertical references differ MUST NOT be combined, assessed after any explicit conversion
     under C-TRANSFORM 3.
   - An input with no declared vertical reference MUST be treated as unestablished, never as agreeing with
     the others.
2. A result whose vertical reference cannot be established MUST NOT be presented as a height relative to any
   surface.
   - It MAY be presented as a raw coordinate value, provided the absence is stated.

#### Rationale

Failing is correct here in a way it rarely is. Every other category of coordinate error announces itself: a
horizontal mismatch puts data in the wrong place, visibly. A vertical datum mismatch produces a correctly
shaped surface at the wrong elevation, and every derived height inherits a constant that no inspection of
the output reveals. The user cannot detect it, so the system must.

The absent case is called out separately in (1) because it is the same failure by a shorter route. LAS files
often declare no vertical reference at all, and treating absence as agreement is how a mismatch becomes
invisible without anyone choosing to ignore it.

(2)'s carve-out matters for usability: refusing to show a number at all would make the tool unusable on data
users consider ordinary. Showing the coordinate while withholding the *interpretation* is the honest middle,
and it is the same distinction [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 3 draws between output and its presentation.

This is the third obligation in this specification with the same shape: [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 2 forbids silent
over-counting, [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) silent approximation, and this silent datum assumption. In each case the
wrong answer is indistinguishable from the right one by inspection, so the discipline has to be structural.

### [RFC-0005:C-BACKEND] Transformation backends and committed results (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-backend"></a>

More than one transformation implementation will exist — a full-featured one requiring a filesystem and a
constrained one that does not — and they will not always agree. A pipeline yielding one answer with the first
wired in and a slightly different answer with the second is exactly the irreproducibility
[RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 2 forbids, so the two cases are separated by how much the answer depends on the
implementation.

1. Exactly one transformation implementation MUST be designated the **reference backend**.
   - The designation MUST be recorded in the project's governed configuration, not inferred from what is
     installed or available at run time.
2. A committed run whose pipeline includes a **datum transformation** MUST use the reference backend.
   - A transformation is a datum transformation when its source and target geodetic datums differ, as
     recorded by the authority registry the reference backend consults.
   - It MUST fail rather than substitute another backend.
3. For transformations that are not datum transformations, any backend MAY be used.
4. For every transformation, whether or not it is a datum transformation, the recorded evaluation
   configuration ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4) MUST include:
   - the backend's identity and version;
   - the version of any transformation database or grid set consulted.
4. A backend that cannot perform a requested transformation MUST fail, naming what it could not do.
   - It MUST NOT substitute a coarser transformation that approximates the request.

#### Rationale

The split in (2) and (3) reflects where implementation dependence actually lives. A map projection is a
closed-form mathematical definition, so two correct implementations agree to floating-point precision and
recording which one ran is sufficient. A **datum transformation** is not: it depends on grid files,
transformation-pipeline selection among several valid candidates, and an authority database encoding which is
preferred for a given area. Two implementations can each be correct and differ by decimetres, and decimetres
of vertical shift is a real error in a canopy metric.

(1)'s recording requirement is what makes the designation checkable rather than ambient. A reference backend
inferred from the environment would vary between machines, which is the opposite of what a reference is for.

(2)'s nested definition exists because the item's gate is mandatory failure, and a precondition an
implementer cannot decide would make the clause either over-fail or under-fail. Characterising the class in
prose — grid files, pipeline selection, an authority database — explains why it matters without saying when
it applies.

(4) covers *every* transformation rather than hanging under (3), which was the earlier arrangement and left
the highest-stakes case uncovered: a committed datum transformation had no clause requiring its grid set
version to be recorded, even though that is exactly the input the rationale says the answer depends on.
Recording the *database and grid versions* matters as much as the backend: the same implementation
with an updated transformation database can legitimately produce a different, better answer, and a result
that cannot say which database produced it is not reproducible even with the same software.

(4) forbids the accommodating behaviour. A constrained backend asked for a transformation it lacks grids for
could apply a coarser equivalent and be approximately right — which is the failure C-VERTICAL exists to
prevent, arriving through a different door.

The practical consequence is that a constrained host cannot produce a committed result involving a datum
shift. That is accepted: such hosts are out of scope, and preview use remains available because previews are
already declared approximate.

### [RFC-0005:C-IDENTITY] Point references (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-identity"></a>

A point reference is a **position in a versioned container**, not a minted identifier. This is free, requires
no sidecar store, and is what both comparable tools use. What makes it safe is not making it durable but
restricting where it may be used.

1. A point reference MUST be the composite of:
   - the source identifier;
   - the source's version fingerprint (C-BINDING);
   - the source's spatial index node key;
   - the point's index within that node.
2. A point reference is valid only for the source version it names.
   - It MUST NOT be interpreted against a different version.
   - It MUST NOT be automatically migrated to one.
3. A point-set edit ([RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 3) MUST attach directly to a source, and MUST NOT appear downstream
   of any operator.
   - A region edit ([RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 2) MAY appear at any position in the document graph.
   - Operators that change cardinality — decimation, voxelisation, filtering, or any reduction — produce
     points that no node key and index address.
4. A per-point identifier MUST NOT be persisted for the general point population.

#### Rationale

(3) is the substantive restriction, and it replaces a problem that first appeared to be about reprojection.
Because [RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 5 makes sources read-only and reprojection is an output concern rather than a
document mutation, reprojection cannot orphan a reference. The real hazard is graph position: an enumerated
reference taken downstream of a cardinality-changing operator is invalidated by a parameter change the user
has every reason to make. Attaching point-set edits to sources only removes that whole class of failure, and
costs little because the enumerated form is the rare escape hatch rather than the default.

(4) forbids the approach that looks most robust and does not scale. A minted identifier per point, persisted
alongside the data, would survive everything — and would require roughly sixteen gigabytes of sidecar for a
billion-point dataset, against a design premise of never materialising the dataset itself. It is phrased as a
prohibition on *persisting* rather than on computing, because an ephemeral internal handle within one
evaluation breaks nothing.

### [RFC-0005:C-BINDING] Source version fingerprint (Normative) <a id="rfc-0005c-binding"></a>

Because edits live beside an immutable source rather than inside it, the two can disagree in a way a
destructive editor cannot experience — there, the file *is* the state. If a source is replaced at the same
location by a reprocessed file, every node key and index still resolves, and now names different points. Point
references would be silently wrong, and [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) would faithfully record an audit trail of
nonsense.

1. Every source MUST be bound to a version fingerprint derived from its bytes.
   - Every point reference MUST name the fingerprint it was taken against (C-IDENTITY 1).
2. The fingerprint MUST be a BLAKE3 digest.
   - Where the format provides a spatial index hierarchy, the digest MUST cover the header and that
     hierarchy.
   - Where it does not, the digest MUST cover the whole file.
3. Fingerprint computation MUST be streaming, with memory independent of file size, in conformance with
   [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 1.
4. On fingerprint mismatch the document MUST open read-only.
   - It MUST identify which edits are bound to the stale fingerprint.
   - It MUST NOT evaluate point-set edits against the mismatched source.
   - It MUST NOT re-resolve their references automatically.
5. A derived artefact — a baked representation, a cache entry, a stored summary — MUST record the fingerprint
   it was derived from, and MUST be invalidated on mismatch.
6. The fingerprint algorithm is part of the persisted document format.
   - A document written by one version MUST remain readable by later versions.
   - Changing how fingerprints are computed MUST be treated as a breaking change to that format.
   - On such a change, stored point references MUST be reported as invalidated, and MUST NOT be silently
     reinterpreted against the new algorithm.

#### Rationale

(2) is a compromise made deliberately rather than an oversight. Digesting a whole 500 GB remote source to
decide whether to trust it reads the entire file, which contradicts the premise of the project more directly
than almost any other single action. The header and hierarchy are small, already fetched in order to traverse
the source at all, and are rewritten by any reprocessing that changes point content — so the cheap digest
catches the realistic case. Formats without a hierarchy offer nothing cheaper than the file, and such sources
are typically indexed on ingest anyway, so the digest rides along on a pass already happening.

The residual gap is named rather than hidden: a byte-level substitution preserving the header and hierarchy
exactly while altering point records would go undetected. Detecting it costs a full read of every source on
every open, which is not a trade this project can make.

BLAKE3 is specified rather than left open because of (6): the digest is not an implementation detail but a
field inside saved documents, so an unspecified algorithm would make a document unreadable by a build that
chose differently. It is used purely as a fast, uniform content digest with no security property intended,
and its streaming construction is what satisfies (3).

(6) is the obligation that makes the algorithm choice consequential, and it is stated here rather than left
as rationale because it is a compatibility rule: it constrains what a future version may do, which no
decision record can enforce. The silent-reinterpretation prohibition is the operative part — a reference
resolving against a new algorithm would name a different point while appearing intact, which is the failure
C-IDENTITY 2 forbids arriving by another route.

(4) preserves every edit while evaluating nothing against stale references, and reports *which* edits are
affected rather than condemning the document — so the user can re-point or discard them deliberately. The
prohibition on automatic re-resolution is the important half: proximity-matching orphaned references is the
one behaviour that would produce a wrong number with no signal.
